The video for Boyfriends begins with a pub landlady (played by the excellent Alyssa Kyria) on the phone telling her friend about the band booked for tonight that she is not happy with. So she has set them up in the pub's toilet with the comment 'the lead singer is a bit of a dick if I'm honest.' We are soon going to find out how right she is. Hard Life - now a fourpiece - are indeed in the toilet and start playing the song, joined by a growing audience of visitors. They are men of a certain age who need to visit the lavatory, but stick around for the band, until it starts getting rather crowded. And then as the rest of the band disappear, the audience attack frontman Murray, revealing his true self underneath... It's unexpected, it's bizarre, and perhaps even slightly shocking. It's certainly a symbol for a gamut of male failings, as Greg Barth explains below. As we are able to share the director's cut here, we can present this specimen in its full unpixellated glory. And as it gets a lot of love from the old guys until the landlady steps in - and sticks the boot in - that certainly makes it more impactful than the version currently on YouTube. Lofsöng and the Language That Outlives Us Editor’s note by Carlos El Asmar Jesse went to Tribeca and came back with a haunted hotel that sings . Now he has brought us singing stones, a shapeshifting piece of origami, and a question about how to speak to people who might exist 100,000 years from now. I’m beginning to see a pattern. What draws me to Lofsöng is the trust it places in the person on the other side of the screen. A shape, a vibration, a patch of light can ask us to stop and work something out for ourselves. I love that. So much of our working life is spent making sure the message lands immediately. Here is a world willing to let us be a little lost. For this next chapter of our , Jesse speaks with Unrelated Studio’s Alessandro Durando about the ideas behind that world, and the people who helped him build it. Put your headphones on for this one. The stones have something to say. On an afternoon at Pier 57, somewhere between the chatter of a dozen playable demos and the steady flow of visitors through the Tribeca Games Gallery, I found myself in front of a screen that refused to speak. No dialogue. No map. No subtitles. Only a small figure in an oversized helmet crossing a gray desert of dust, an origami companion folding itself into the wind, and enormous concrete monuments waiting to be heard. 2026 Tribeca Games official selection , a team based in Turin, Italy. Its creative director, , sat down with me to explain how a nuclear waste repository in Finland, the idea of speaking architecture, and a Sardinian sculptor who taught stones to sing all ended up inside the same piece of software. You explore by listening, singing to sculptures, and discovering how mechanisms respond. Your origami companion reshapes itself to carry you across the Dust Sea, becoming a kite, a glider, a sailboat, and new forms appear as the world opens up. items.page_excerpt: DN & BIFA Present: 2026 Best British Short Film Nominee Screening & Q+A have arrived, and ahead of the winner being revealed next month, Directors Notes is bringing all five Best British Short Film nominees together on one screen. On Wednesday 25th November, from 6pm in Hackney, London for an evening with the BIFA shorts and the people who made them. This year’s nominated list moves from a UK asylum hotel to a West Bank road at night, from a 1988 journey to space to an art class confrontation and arrives on the campaign trail of a would-be MP. Together, the five films make a strong case for what British short filmmaking can achieve… and the results are impressive as hell! We’re not stopping at the credits. (Hasan Kattan, Orlando von Einsiedel) An intimate documentary in which a friendship forged on the frontlines of the Syrian revolution meets the airless limbo of a UK asylum hotel, as Hasan and co-director Fadi Al Halabi turn their cameras on each other. items.page_excerpt: Elham Ehsas On His “Duty” To Tell Afghanistan’s Space Story in BIFA Nominated Short ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ When we think of films about Afghanistan, we’re often drawn to stories shaped by the country’s near-continuous experience of conflict over the past 40+ years. Even a quick image search tends to confirm this perception, presenting a familiar catalogue of violence and instability. While these stories are undoubtedly important, their dominance has created an increasingly narrow picture of a country whose history and culture extend far beyond its troubled recent past. Seeking to challenge this limited perspective is , whose BIFA-nominated short, , revisits an extraordinary but largely overlooked moment in Afghan history: the journey of Abdul Ahad Momand, the country’s first and only astronaut. “When I tell people that an Afghan has been to space, they don’t believe me,” Ehsas states in the film’s voiceover. It’s a revealing observation that speaks not only to the obscurity of Momand’s achievement, but also to the media representation that continues to shape how Afghanistan is viewed internationally. However, beyond restoring Momand’s place in the historical record, Ehsas’ memorable short film also develops into something more personal, connecting this remarkable chapter of Afghan history to his own family and understanding of home. Keen to explore the motivations behind the project and the personal discoveries that emerged during its making, we invited Ehsas to join us on Directors Notes as part of our BIFA nominees interview series to discuss the ideas and creative process behind screens alongside the four other BIFA Best British Short Film nominees at DN and BIFA’s nominees screening on Wednesday 25 November at Lanzarote Works, 230 Dalston Lane, London E8 1LA. items.description: Some histories refuse to stay buried. Celeste Diep confronts the generational scars of Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge past in her deeply affecting short.
items.page_excerpt: Haunted Histories, Living Ghosts: Celeste Diep Explores Cambodia’s Generational Wounds in ‘Interview with a Hero’ The weight of history is not always something that can be spoken about, but it can be shown, or it can come out in unexpected ways or times. For many Cambodian people, the trauma of the Khmer Rouge regime, the genocide and the generations of silence that followed remain an ever-present burden, passed down through families and carried into everyday life. In Australian Film Television and Radio School (AFTRS) , that inherited pain becomes the starting point for a deeply affecting story about generational trauma and diaspora, centred on Chhay, a man whose buried past threatens his relationships with his family and community. The short caught my eye some time ago, and was part of my selection, so it feels completely natural to welcome the film to our pages for its premiere. Recently, Taz F. Stark’s hit me in a similar way with its portrayal of this historical tragedy when I highlighted it in my HollyShorts UK Best of Fest – a powerful thematic shorts pairing that would not be for the faint of heart. Joining Directors Notes for online release, Diep digs deep into the process of bringing the past back to life, opens up about the emotional toll of revisiting such a painful chapter of Cambodian history and explains her fascinating use of shadow puppetry to bring its story to life. Writing a “self-insert” daughter means you are simultaneously acting as the objective director, the subjective writer, and the real-world daughter. That requires an intense amount of emotional gymnastics. How did you manage to maintain enough narrative distance while talking about such a personal story? It’s always been in my mind to tell this story from a young age (although I hadn’t known as a child that film would be the medium). I’ve always had this burning desire to make a film about my local Cambodian diaspora, and to particularly make a film inspired by my father. Much of it takes place and is shot in my local community in Bonnyrigg, Sydney, where I grew up and met other Cambodian children and adults. items.page_excerpt: Camille Summers-Valli Confronts the Invisibility of Female Ageing in Precisely Composed BIFA Short ‘Untitled Woman’ A particular kind of invisibility comes with growing older as a woman, especially in a culture that so often equates female worth with youth, beauty and desirability. It is this experience that –which we first highlighted as part of our BFI London Film Festival Best of Fest selection last month–captures so well and so delicately. Through a strikingly literal interpretation of the desire to be seen, filmmaker turns an everyday yet rarely acknowledged experience into a compelling visual exploration of the necessity to regain power while ageing. Through the lens of its protagonist, Dawn, we are asked a deceptively simple but increasingly resonant question: what does it mean to be seen in a world where images mean everything? Pixar alum Connie He on turning insomnia into a six-minute short, tuning a model to her own concept art, and what it took for animators and researchers to speak the same language. Dear Upstairs Neighbors had its world premiere as part of Whoopi’s Wonderful World of Animation at the 2026 Tribeca Festival. Motionographer was in the theater for every short in the program, and this article is part of our series dedicated to the films of this year’s lineup, with more on the way. Dear Upstairs Neighbors. Courtesy of the filmmakers Somewhere in the middle of our conversation, Connie He stopped explaining how she conceived and directed and started marveling at it, as if she were discovering the film for the first time. She was describing the earliest tests she and her team ran on a video model trained on their own concept art. The model picked up a low camera angle nobody had asked for. It picked up the zigzag lines the team drew wherever an object touched the ground, and nobody had told it those lines mattered. “We’re like, oh my god, it’s picking up on all those patterns that we didn’t even think of. That’s kind of an aha moment. We’re like, okay, I think what we are thinking is actually possible.” More than anything else she told me, that moment holds the essence of , the six-minute animated short that previewed at Sundance in January, had its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival in June, and went on to SIGGRAPH in July. STUDIO STORIES: Tonic DNA, The Studio That Refused to Be One Thing This Studio Story was reported the way most of our lives now happen: on a screen, between New York and Montreal. One long conversation over Zoom at the end of August, recorded, followed by a written questionnaire that Stefanie Bitton answered in her own voice and at her own pace over the weeks that followed. I had cancelled on her twice. When we finally spoke I was running on cold medicine, she was running a studio, and neither of us was willing to cancel a third time. I am glad we did not, because what came through that screen was not a pitch. It was a partner who has spent twenty years inside a studio twice that old, talking about drawings, phone calls, a beaver, a penguin-powered Santa and the people at the desks, with the same steadiness whether the subject was an Oscar or a spreadsheet. What I did not expect was the candor. Twice in that hour she corrected my premise without apology: no, this is a refresh, not a rebrand, and no, 2D never went anywhere, so there is nothing to bring back. When she did not have an answer she said so, and when we reached the film that still makes her cry she let the pause do the talking. A partner with four decades of studio history behind her and nothing to oversell is a rare interview, and it made this piece a pleasure to write. items.page_excerpt: Fostering The Motion Design Community Since 2006. The Motion Awards 2025 Winners! The Haunted Hotel That Sings Back: Anil Glendinning on There Are No Ghosts at the Grand continues with Jesse Rylander’s conversation with Anil Glendinning, co-founder and creative director of , the studio behind There Are No Ghosts at the Grand. Jesse met Glendinning at Tribeca Games in June and played the game on the gallery floor at Pier 57. What follows is his account. There Are No Ghosts at the Grand, inside the greenhouse. Courtesy of Friday Sundae. Some games tell you their genre in a word. There Are No Ghosts at the Grand needs a whole breath. When I sat down with Anil Glendinning at Tribeca Games, he described it, without blinking, as “a musical, narrative, renovation, horror, comedy, story game.” After spending time with it on the gallery floor at Pier 57, I understood why he didn’t bother trimming the list. Every one of those words is doing work. The setup is simple enough. You play Chris David, an American who inherits a crumbling seaside hotel in England from the British side of a family he has never met. By day, you restore the Grand and the sleepy village around it with a toolkit of increasingly bizarre power tools, some of which talk back. By night, those same tools turn into ghost-hunting gear. There is also a sardonic cat. And, at unpredictable moments, the people of the town break into song. Glendinning is co-founder and creative director of Friday Sundae, a UK studio of just ten people, and he co-directs the game with producer Rachel Glendinning. The game had its world premiere at Tribeca in June 2026 and won the , the festival’s prize for excellence in artistic storytelling, chosen from 12 official selections. Our conversation made it clear that nearly every choice in it, from the textures to the soundtrack, traces back to one idea: a ghost story should feel like a memory. Players at the Tribeca Games gallery, Pier 57, New York. Photo: Jesse Rylander. A ghost story built from a childhood When the team began writing, Glendinning said, they went back to the places that had frightened them as kids. Not haunted mansions, but something more specific and more British.

La lumière transforme l’architecture contemporaine en émotion. Découvrez comment elle façonne les espaces, les villes et le quotidien pour les usagers. La lumière ne se contente pas d’éclairer l’architecture contemporaine : elle lui donne du sens, du relief, et suscite des émotions. Naturel ou artificiel, l’éclairage façonne la perception des lieux dans nos vies. Il améliore le confort et valorise les usages. En bref, il rend les architectures vivantes, mais aussi plus durables et plus humaines. [Article mis à jour le : 07/09/2026] Qu’est-ce que l’architecture contemporaine ? L’architecture contemporaine est l’art de concevoir des espaces de vie où la lumière joue un rôle central . Il ne s’agit pas que des sols, des murs et des matières ! Les pour créer des expériences uniques. items.page_excerpt: Fostering The Motion Design Community Since 2006. The Motion Awards 2025 Winners! I’M HAVING A BREAKDOWN: DREAMCAT, the monster that wasn’t his I cannot tell you how DREAMCAT found me. I don’t have social media, and the morning of our call I was still trying to remember who sent it. What I do remember is the behind-the-scenes video. Something clicked, and when something makes me feel something, I pursue it. People need to know what happened to this film after the shoot, when the one they thought they had quietly turned into a different one. That is the story a press release cannot tell, and it is the reason this series exists. When I saw a studio in Düsseldorf and an animator in Brussels spend almost three years on a film combining live action and hand-drawn animation, then throw away two weeks of that drawing because it wasn’t true to the man on screen, I felt something I hadn’t felt in a while. Then I met them, on a Friday night at nine o’clock their time, beers in hand, and I couldn’t believe it either. This is what I’m Having a Breakdown is for. Danny, Joost and Jakob opened the drawers: the plates, the scrapped monster, the Jedi shot that got cut down, the raw drawings and the finished frames. Here is the film they made, and the one they didn’t. The making of DREAMCAT. Courtesy of MAKE MAMI PROUD and Joost Jansen. The monster that wasn’t his Joost Jansen had spent roughly two weeks animating a monster for a film about himself. Then he said it did not belong there. Director Daniel “Danny” Bartels had been bracing for that conversation. Two weeks of drawing were in the cut, and he was still working out how to raise it without hurting his friend. He never had to. items.page_excerpt: Top Ten Designers in Paris Nowness Picks: Top Ten Designers in Paris Issey Miyake and Marithé + François Girbaud lead an exclusive clip from the 1980 fashion documentary, shooting the Paris runway and its icons in up-close detail Shot on Super 8 and 16mm film by collaborative collective Soft Ware Productions – a fake production company dreamed up by filmmakers Vivian Ostrovsky, Nicole Deschaumes, Olivier Guiton, Philippe Grandrieux, Jérôme de Missolz, and Evelyne Ragot – archival fashion film Top Ten Designers in Paris captures the Spring/Summer 1980 collections through some of the era’s leading fashion houses, between candid interviews and intimate runway moments. It’s a lot about body language. So, when you look back from today’s point of view, certain things come to the forefront that you hadn’t expected: the design of interiors, the way people are dressed, the way they move. Amplifying the textures and gestures of catwalk presentations by Issey Miyake, Karl Lagerfeld, Angelo Tarlazzi, Tan Giudicelli, Jean-Paul Gaulthier, Marithé + François Girbaud, France Andrévie, Claude Montana, Kenzo and Thierry Mugler, the film lifts the curtain on a defining moment in 20th century fashion, and the design talent that helped shaped it. In an exclusive excerpt from the full-length film, revisit the energy, intimacy, and euphoria of 1979 Paris, and the visionary spirit that marked a generation, illuminating its greatest icons in ultra-close proximity. Face à quatre grands écrans recto-verso de projection immersive, le visiteur est d'abord scanné pour faire entrer sa carnation dans l'œuvre, puis joue avec les données : chaque point représente une carnation captée par Sephora dans ses boutiques au Canada, donnant à voir d'un seul regard toute la diversité des peaux du pays. Comme creative tech producer, j'ai orchestré la chaîne temps réel (LIDAR SICK, TouchDesigner, moteur Notch, diffusion ETC OnlyView) et le son spatialisé signé Start-Rec. Une œuvre au message fort sur la diversité et l'inclusion. 4 grands écrans recto-verso de projection immersive. Data de carnations captées en boutiques au Canada. Pour l'interactivité, des LIDAR SICK captent les mouvements du public devant les écrans et lui permettent de jouer avec les données en temps réel. Ces flux sont traités sous TouchDesigner, qui héberge un moteur Notch pour la gestion des particules, le rendu étant diffusé via un système ETC OnlyView. La diffusion audio spatialisée, signée Start-Rec, repose sur Ableton et Max MSP en temps réel. En amont, une borne scanne la carnation des visiteurs pour les faire entrer dans l'œuvre.

items.page_excerpt: New York filmmaker Guy Kozak captures advice on love, life and fishing in Cape Cod, exploring male friendship traditions on 16mm film For the short film Fishing Lessons, New York-based filmmaker Guy Kozak reflects on romantic relationships through angling and the traditions of male bonding, creating an intimate memento to mark his first wedding anniversary. Shooting over one day in Cape Cod – where his wife grew up and where they were married the previous year – Kozak cast his stepfather-in-law Nat, and his closest friends, Bo & Bill, to deliver their advice on love, life, and fishing, captured against the stillness of the coastal landscape. The fishermen are my stepfather-in-law, and his good friends. I wanted to capture their reflections on life and love, as well as the landscape itself, creating a souvenir that I might look back on as I move forward in my own life and relationship. Working with five rolls of expired 16mm film, Kozak embraces the unpredictability and warping of an imperfect medium, while mirroring the uncertainties of both fishing and human connection. Drawing inspiration from the poetic documentary-style of U.S. filmmaker Les Blank, Kozak frames the fishing tradition as a shared space for peace and reflection, highlighting the intimacy, sentimentality and gentleness often missing from portrayals of masculinity. items.page_excerpt: Top Ten Designers in Paris Top Ten Designers in Paris Director Felix Aaron explores queer isolation, memory, and the need to be seen yet invisible from the winter landscape of Portrush, Northern Ireland, with Berlin-based fashion brand Dagger Shaped by memories of growing up in a seaside town defined by two very different seasons, Berlin-based fashion brand Dagger and director Felix Aaron expand the autobiographical story behind its Autumn/Winter 2026 collection PLAY HARD for the short film – premiered at Dover Street Market Paris. Rooted in Dagger founder and creative director Luke Rainey’s upbringing in Portrush, Northern Ireland, GHOSTS frames a town transformed by tourism in summer before disappearing crowds give way to a winter landscape of empty amusement arcades, emptier beaches, rain, sea fog and streets built around now-absent crowds. I wrote GHOSTS about the total isolation I felt as a queer teenager growing up in Portrush in the early 2000s. It’s about wanting desperately to be seen by someone, while at the same time trying as hard as possible not to be. Observing boredom as a creative force among the young people who call the town home, captures the drive to construct a world within a place that can feel forgotten, exploring themes of queer isolation, memory, and the desire to be seen while trying to disappear. Caught between memory and fiction, the film explores youth and belonging through the “ghosts” of friendships, loves, landscape and versions of ourselves that remain attached to where we grew up. In an excerpt from the 21-minute, six-channel video, enter a virtual universe that brings together music, choreography, and animation in ecstatic scenes that celebrate hope, joy, and liberation. Satterwhite’s time-based piece echoes the grammar of endless-runner video games but eschews the gratuitous violence and exploitation that is common to this genre. Channeling the Buddhist Metta prayer of loving-kindness, the artist creates a mantra of his own, inspired by queer freedom of existence and expression. features Satterwhite collaborators including musicians Solange Knowles, Kelsey Lu and Moses Sumney, as well as drag artist Laveau Contraire, queer wrestling collective Choke Hole, and dance artist O'Shae Sibley. L’ensemble de ces dispositions adoptées en première lecture reste soumis à la poursuite de la navette parlementaire et ne revêt donc, à ce stade, aucun caractère définitif. Avec un avis favorable de la commission des finances, le gouvernement s’en remettant « à la sagesse du Sénat », selon la formule consacrée, les sénateurs ont adopté six amendements identiques ( supprimant l’abattement de 66% dont bénéficient les plateformes gratuites de partage de vidéos au titre de la taxe sur les recettes publicitaires des services d’accès à des contenus audiovisuels à la demande (TSV-G). Le projet initial du Gouvernement prévoyait de ramener cet abattement à 33%. Sa suppression intégrale devrait générer, selon la commission des finances du Sénat, quelque 35 M€ de recettes supplémentaires pour le Centre national du cinéma et de l’image animée (CNC) par rapport au dispositif gouvernemental. Dans leurs exposés des motifs, les sénateurs font valoir que la justification économique de cet abattement, instauré en 2016 pour tenir compte de la part importante des contenus amateurs sur ces plateformes, n’est désormais plus pertinente.
